entries.title: Dudes Online Are So Mad That ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Makes Them Respect Women
entries.summary: Much to the dismay of right-wing streamers, being a thoughtful boyfriend is key to the game’s storyline.
entries.content:
The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)

More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

And Andrew Tate himself denounced the game in a Thursday email blast to his newsletter subscribers. “The establishment does not understand the male spirit,” he wrote from prison in Miami, where he and his brother Tristan Tate are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape, human trafficking, and assault. “No man wants to be a slave who breaks his back and gets nothing back.” Promoting a link to classes for building “AI systems,” he exhorted his readers: “Put down the game controller.”

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.)

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.

It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

entries.title: Best Amazon Black Friday Deals (2026)
entries.summary: For die-hard Amazon shoppers, the retailer is starting Black Friday early. You can shop the deals from now until November 30.
entries.content:
Amazon’s Black Friday deals are now live. Its “Black Friday Week” sale runs November 19–30 (Cyber Monday), giving shoppers a head start on holiday shopping. The retailer has already discounted many items since last week and has now added even more to the sale. Even better, we’re seeing some items with even lower prices. To help you sift through the products, we’ve highlighted some of our favorites below. If you’re a big Amazon shopper, now is a great time to fill those holiday wish lists and spend Black Friday with friends and family.

Check out our guide to the best Early Black Friday deals, plus standing desk deals, Home Depot appliance savings, and early tech deals.

Updated November 19: Amazon’s Black Friday deals start today. We’ve updated this story to reflect that and added more products we’ve recommended in our guides and reviews.

Best Amazon Black Friday Tech Deals

With a WIRED rating of 9 out of 10, the XM6 is one of our favorite over-ear headphones, combining comfort with great sound quality and noise cancellation. This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

Good gaming laptops are never cheap, and they’ve become even more expensive this year. If you need a recommendation that balances performance and budget, we recommend the Asus ROG Strix G16 with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, one of our favorite budget gaming laptops. We prefer the RTX 5070 option, but it’s nearly $3,000. This on-sale model is more attainable.

The latest Echo Show 11 is our recommendation for the Best Alexa Smart Display. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found the screen bright and crisp, with immersive sound quality. Since the sale price matches the regular price of the smaller Echo Show 8, it’s a good deal—just $5 more than the sale price during Amazon’s October Prime Day event.

The Pixel 11-series phones from Google are among our favorite Android devices. Loaded with the latest software and Gemini AI features, the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL are our pick as the smartest Android smartphones. They’re also the only non-iPhones to support Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic mounting, so you can use MagSafe accessories. During Black Friday, you can get all for under $1,000 each—a terrific deal for a flagship phone—and they’re at their lowest price ever on Amazon.

The Series 12 model is not only cheaper than the high-end Ultra 4, but it’s also the best Apple Watch you can buy, period. It has the latest health-sensing features, including a Readiness score that summarizes your recent health and activity. Its Amazon sale price is currently the lowest since its introduction.

High-quality three-in-one charging stands look terrific on a bedside table, but many cost over $100. This one from Mophie is one of our favorites, and it’s 49 percent off on Amazon right now.

The AirTag seems to be on sale all the time, but no matter—it’s currently the lowest price on Amazon and cheaper than buying from Apple. It’s one of the best Bluetooth trackers. If you can swing it, go for the four-pack.

Alongside the AirTag, the AirPods Max 2 and AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale. These are well-regarded among WIRED testers, but we recommend waiting until after Thanksgiving to see if they drop further—don’t worry, they are often on sale.

Phone accessories are aplenty on Amazon, but few look as good as Moft’s. You can pick up this ingenious wallet-kickstand hybrid that attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe, or peruse the rest of Moft's Black Friday deals.

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our short list, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s you, it’s NBD. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $40, but it’s 50 percent off right now.

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boom box in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

This EcoFlow portable battery is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s pick as the best power bank for laptops. It has a large 27,650-mAh capacity, which is plenty for charging smaller devices too. It’s great for travel since it’s allowed on a plane, and it has a retractable USB-C cable, so you can leave extras at home.

At $359, the second-gen Bose QuietComfort over-ear headphones seem overpriced considering the competition. But when they’re on sale at $199 to $219 (depending on the color), they suddenly become a great buy. As expected from Bose, the noise cancellation and sound quality are excellent. They are also comfortable, making them great travel companions. Note that the first-gen version is also on sale for $169 (it’s frequently at this price), but it’s outdated, and we think you should spend $30 to $50 more on the latest version instead.

Amazon Early Black Friday Home and Kitchen Deals

Love them or hate them, but pod-based coffee makers are popular for their convenience. The Nespresso Vertuo Pop+ is our recommended espresso pod maker, and the Deluxe model is under $100. It has a larger water tank than the standard version, and the Vertuo pods are recyclable. For more savings on coffee-related products, check out our Early Black Friday Espresso Machine Deals.

WIRED’s home-cleaning expert, Nena Farrell, recommended only three robot vacuums, naming this Eufy floor-sweeping automaton her budget pick. It’s 43 percent off right now for a robovac with great suction power and a self-cleaning roller mop.

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.

entries.title: What’s With All These Outages?
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we discuss the outages that have swept digital life over the past week, where new money from Anthropic’s IPO is going, and the AI chip world post-Jensen Huang.
entries.content:
Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and the administration’s new rule to stop Chinese companies from renting AI chips just before Trump meets Xi.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Sophie Kleeman on X/Twitter at @sophiekleeman, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Hey, this is Brian. If you've been listening for a while and you haven't rated or reviewed the podcast yet, this is your sign. Give us a rating. Tell us what you think. Five stars is nice, but we'll take the feedback too. It really helps more people find the show. OK, on to the show. So, hey everybody, I want to say, first of all, we've got a very special guest today in the studio with Leah. It's Sophie Kleeman.

Leah Feiger: Woo-hoo. Sophie's here.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm here.

Brian Barrett: Sophie is our senior editor on the business desk, and we're so glad to have her. And I've heard that she is going to do a lot of yelling and pointing and just anger I think is her vibe, is what I've been told, coming in.

Sophie Kleeman: Yes. Let's get started.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Sophie Kleeman: And I am Sophie Kleeman, senior business editor.

Brian Barrett: This week we're discussing why everything seems to be breaking down all the time. First, it was Microsoft, then the FAA and air traffic control. Then Chase Bank, United Airlines, the NSA, Apple, the tech outages have been piling up and raising questions around what caused them, and why they're happening all at the same time, seemingly. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says that we are not under attack. He's right, but the internet is not convinced. We'll get into what actually went wrong and why a lot of people's first instinct is to blame hackers and AI in some combination.

Sophie Kleeman: And I am one of those people, so can't wait to get into that. We will also take a look at Anthropic officially going public this week. It will be one of the biggest IPOs ever, but the timing is a little bit complicated. So we will talk about who's about to get very, very rich and whether the recent midterm results could impact the company's grand ambitions.

Brian Barrett: And in other AI news, we're going to have a quick NVIDIA update as the company just released the first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm and had their first all-hands led by interim CEO Colette Kress.

Leah Feiger: We're also going to be checking in on President Donald Trump's visit to Asia, specifically China, which comes just days after his administration has moved to close a loophole that lets Chinese companies access AI chips. We're going to talk about what the Nvidia scandal has had to do with all of this and the fight inside the administration over how to handle everything.

Brian Barrett: All right look, if you picked up your phone at any point in last week to look at the news, if you went to wired.com at any point last week or anywhere on social media, you were hit with news that something somewhere had an outage.

Leah Feiger: Brian, everything is broken.

Brian Barrett: Everything's broken.

Leah Feiger: Every single thing is broken.

Brian Barrett: Everything's broken and breaking, increasingly fixed. I want to walk through this really quickly. I know people are tired of it, the so many things. We're going to list off some of the biggest ones, OK? Last Thursday, Microsoft had an outage in Outlook and Teams that was about 24 hours, which is incredibly long for those services to be out when the whole world basically depends on them to communicate. The next day, Friday, the FAA had a ground stop for the entire country, only the second time that has happened since 9/11, and it was the longest one since then. It was for more than four hours. Then on Monday, everyone said that their banks no longer worked. It turns out to be JP Morgan Chase specifically had a problem, but because banks are all counterparties to each other, every bank had an issue. If one bank had an issue, that same day, United delayed more than a hundred flights for a separate issue. Then on Tuesday, the NSA's classified internal network went down and just for good measure, an internal update also knocked out iCloud and Apple Pay for not quite as long, not quite as dramatically, but throw it on the pile. Now I want to be clear, every single one of these companies and agencies and organizations has said the incidents were not cyberattacks. It was not some combination of a ruthless AI agent and Iranian hackers. There's no evidence that any of these clustered tech failures were even related aside from the bank thing, which is self-contained in the banking industry, but that hasn't stopped people from being suspicious, trying to find a through line, and I think getting on their conspiracy horses. And Sophie, you've been riding one at the front of the battle.

Sophie Kleeman: Yes, I sure have.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. How are you taking all of this in so I can debunk it?

Sophie Kleeman: OK. So I would like to say first off that I do think this has sort of trickled down into people who don't follow this super closely.

Leah Feiger: I mean, it had to. This was your emails, this was your banking, these were your flights.

Sophie Kleeman: Right. Everyone's talking about this.

Leah Feiger: This is it.

Sophie Kleeman: To give you two very, very, very distinct examples, yesterday my fantasy football group chat blew up because someone was like, "Hey guys who follow this, and who are paying attention, are we under attack?" And Brian, you'll be proud of me. I actually said you should read wired.com for the answer to that.

Brian Barrett: Good job, Sophie.

Leah Feiger: She did not say, "Yes, go to the bunkers." Which I know is what you wanted to say.

Sophie Kleeman: It is what I wanted to say.

Leah Feiger: Look, I will say though, I get that inclination. These are so many public services that everyone has really just taken for granted, not only to work, but to help us function in our day-to-day lives. I talked to friends who were like, "Oh yeah, I just had a day and a half off of work basically, and then could not pay my rent." It was everything.

Brian Barrett: And there are people who are doing doomsday prepping at Costco now. I've had multiple group chats where people, even when I've told them, "Hey, it's actually fine," they are still prepping their bunkers. I think it's instructive. I have covered outages for a long time at WIRED because I think they're fascinating because they affect so many people, and they have such mundane causes usually. So I want to talk through a couple of things and what happened. Just for any listeners who are still worried about it, they all have very distinct things. The Microsoft Outlook issue was actually ... I love this one. It was a fix that was deployed in July. They basically made an update in July, propagated it out, but was not triggered until last week. Something else happened.

Sophie Kleeman: Do we know what that something else is? I'm just asking questions.

Brian Barrett: Iranian hackers. No, they've done a shorter postmortem. They're going to do a longer postmortem. The gist of it was they pushed this thing out and then it propagated out through the whole network and then they had another update. They stepped on the landmine and everything went boom, and it took a while to correct. For the FAA, when air traffic control went down, and Aarian Marshall, who covers transportation mobility for us here at WIRED, was very early to say this doesn't seem like hackers. There was a lot of suspicion there because the FAA just the day before had rolled out an AI system to help with air traffic control. The difference is that system's more about data, and about where planes are going and what they're doing. The system that was affected, the problem on Friday, was that people couldn't talk to each other. It was a comms issue. And that tied back to old, old, old fiber equipment that a company called L3Harris maintains. They were trying to push an update on Friday afternoon, which you never do. That's the crazy part to me is that they were trying to push—

Leah Feiger: It's the perfect time.

Sophie Kleeman: Yeah.

Brian Barrett: Push an update to production on a Friday, a couple weeks before Thanksgiving? Crazy stuff.

Leah Feiger: And then I mean the rest was all the same too, right Brian? Chase blamed a software bug in their own hardware. United said it was a technology related issue. NSA blamed routine maintenance. Apple blamed an internal update. All of this was kind of the same. It was just all happening at the same time.

Sophie Kleeman: At the same time.

Leah Feiger: But I think I get it. I get the fears here. I also understand the timing in some ways. We're nearing the end of the year. People need to push all of these updates before holiday travel season or just holiday banking season, I guess, email season.

Sophie Kleeman: Email season.

Leah Feiger: But it is understandable that everyone went straight to the hackers, straight to AI overlords because we've actually been having a not small amount of those examples. If you had told me that this was another Hugging Face incident, I would've been like, yep. Alright. Sounds good.

Sophie Kleeman: You're like, yeah, that sounds right.

Brian Barrett: Well, and Leah too, I think what doesn't help, there's the political dimension here too, because Markwayne Mullin can tell me everything's fine, all he wants. I don't necessarily buy anything from him.

Sophie Kleeman: I don't believe him.

Brian Barrett: Right. I inherently, this administration has no credibility. So in these moments, what do we do?

Leah Feiger: I have to shout out our podcast producer right now. Obviously we are sitting here with a list of notes about all of this and I just quickly looked at it and one tab line was, also people don't trust the government.

Sophie Kleeman: Incredible.

Leah Feiger: Which is, yeah, that is the situation right now. That is perhaps the most succinct, accurate way to push this, which is there was just a massive referendum a few weeks ago. Dems are coming in, guns blazing, and everything is breaking right before that happens. I get it.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm the devil's advocate here, right? I was the person last week where I was like, we're all going to die. We're under attack. This is crazy. This is all happening at the same time. Obviously I don't think that that's really the case, but I will say that I do think two things. I think people are quick to blame AI for things because they don't like it, they don't understand it, they are scared of it, and the companies who are selling it are not doing a great job of selling their product in ways that make people want to sort of feel good about themselves. But the second point is that it was AI, right? It was just the flip side of it. It was like, these companies are deploying these incredibly advanced systems to find vulnerabilities, to find issues within their very complex and in some cases old systems and they're finding it and then they're patching it all at the same time. And that's what I think that reporting has suggested that's what we're seeing.

Brian Barrett: This goes back to Anthropic's Mythos model, which is very good at cybersecurity. You might remember it from such news headlines as Anthropic gets banned from the Pentagon and other stupid moments in AI history. Mythos is very, very good at cybersecurity. Anthropic gave access to a limited number, actually a decent number of people who control sensitive information, governments, organizations, companies, and those companies have since been using it to identify bugs that they couldn't find otherwise. Sending patches at a huge rate, and the more complicated the bug, the more patches trying to push out at the same time, the more likely something is going to break. And I think that's what we're seeing here. So yeah, AI plays a role, but in some ways you can think of this as companies trying to get ahead of the hacking version of this. They're doing this because otherwise, in a few months, someone's going to actually say, oh, we can break into the air traffic control system, shut it down ourselves.

Leah Feiger: Right.

Sophie Kleeman: Am I the only one who would love to see that? What if we just went offline forever? What if it all shut down? That would be great. We could all touch grass.

Brian Barrett: I think that'd be great.

Sophie Kleeman: Finally.

Leah Feiger: All right.

Brian Barrett: I think it'd be great.

Sophie Kleeman: Thank you Brian.

Brian Barrett: It would affect the podcast, but that's OK. We can mail each other letters.

Leah Feiger: I've been tickled, though, by all of these comments from our government officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has tried really hard to kind of de-escalate this as well, claiming there's no foul play. He's traveling with Trump in Asia this week, and he said in a press conference multiple times, "We are not under systemic attack."

Marco Rubio, archival audio: The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever. We have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other.

Leah Feiger: And Trump had a different take. I was slightly less reassured.

Archival audio: Are you concerned about all these outages? Microsoft, the FAA, United, Chase Bank?

Donald Trump, archival audio: No. It's life. When you're big and powerful, and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine.

Leah Feiger: OK. The reason I had to pivot to that is that's perhaps like the Sophie model here. You're like, "Yeah, shut it down. This is it. This is what we've signed up for."

Sophie Kleeman: You know what? We're just going to roll with it.

Leah Feiger: Sophie and Trump, two peas in a pod.

Sophie Kleeman: We are such similar people in so many ways. In other news, it's been a crazy week, hasn't it? So Anthropic finally arrived on the stock market. The company's long-awaited IPO debut started trading under the ticker ANT, which I would just like to say is actually very cute. And it's valued at a reported one and a half trillion dollars, which is just a staggering, staggering number. It is among the biggest IPOs ever, but it is actually below the $2 trillion figure that was floating around several months ago. And since then, things have shifted even more. Nvidia lost its CEO and about $2 trillion in market value. And in the midterms, voters overwhelmingly rejected provisions that supported data centers that AI companies need. So given this interesting, interesting timing, what are we looking for?

Brian Barrett: I am looking for a lot of people to become insanely wealthy, even if it's slightly less insanely wealthy than it would've been a couple of months ago.

Sophie Kleeman: Just slightly less.

Brian Barrett: Just slightly, just like a little tiny bit.

Sophie Kleeman: To be clear, $1.5 trillion is still ...

Brian Barrett: It's still generational wealth, but how many generations are we talking about? Trick question. Anthropic doesn't care because they all think we're going to die in the next 10 years or so because of AI. Sophie, I'm curious what you think, because when I think of the Anthropic IPO, which I do every day, every day I'm thinking Anthropic IPO.

Sophie Kleeman: You wake up in the morning and you think Anthropic IPO.

Brian Barrett: I think ANT, ANT, ANT. But it's the first, not the first, it's the biggest pure-play AI IPO that we've had and maybe that we're going to have depending on what happens with OpenAI. SpaceX had an IPO recently, but that is a rocket company with an AI company stapled to it. So what do you look for when this company goes public and people can trade on it? How much do we look at it as a bellwether for the industry in general? Not on the first day of trading even, but just in general, how much can we look and say, oh, that's how the AI industry is going?

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think it is the bellwether, right? It is the first, it is enormous. It's such a leader in the space. And I think that the interesting thing to me is how much it is connected to the other sort of giants in the space, which is to say Amazon and Google, and a few other companies. I mean, those two firms are themselves going to make a shit ton of money from this IPO. They have, what is it? 15 percent. Amazon will own 15 percent. Google will own nearly 14 percent. Those are huge numbers. So I think just this idea that all the financing is tied together and all of these people are riding on the same rocket ship that may or may not crash onto the surface of the earth.

Brian Barrett: And not just that, but Anthropic, they're like a rent-not-own approach to data centers. So they've got nearly a trillion dollars of data center commitments that is all going to other companies. It is sort of fueling, whether that's SpaceX or Google. So they are such a symbol of the interdependency of this industry. And again, can't stress this enough, they are pretty sure that AI will destroy everything, and think that their best chance to make a trillion dollars is to build the kind of AI that will destroy everything as fast as they can. It's in their prospectus.

Sophie Kleeman: Only they can prevent mass AI destruction. The other thing I would like to sort of cite here: I feel like with these IPO stories, obviously everyone's sort of focused on the money, and the What does it mean? and blah, blah, blah. But one kind of very weird fun fact that I would like to just highlight here is that Sam Bankman-Fried of all of this. He was supposed to make money on this because he was invested in Anthropic, but when he went through his bankruptcy and all of his legal problems, the government clawed back that investment.

Leah Feiger: Wait, so where are his shares now? Love that.

Sophie Kleeman: They got sold to some people for a very little amount of money, and now those people are going to be rich.

Leah Feiger: Oh, that's fun. That's a fun thing to follow.

Sophie Kleeman: Highly recommend checking that out.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. Look, you guys know me. I'm interested in this from a political standpoint. Voters voted against data centers. Politicians won their campaigns by promising that data centers were out across the board. This was bipartisan, this was Republican, this was Democrat. So as Anthropic is entering this space, as other companies, OpenAI, etc., are kind of watching how this goes for them, I'm really curious in the coming months what these investments in data centers is going to mean for them. I wonder if it's going to mean slowdowns. I wonder if any of these newly electeds will actually be able to hold these folks accountable. We're going to see, but there is very much a question mark for me there about what comes next.

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think one of the great things for us as journalists too about this IPO is Anthropic will now be a public company. So they are much more accountable and accountable in ways that we can actually dig into and go through their 10-Ks and go through their 10-Qs and all the rest of it. They're going to have to do earnings calls and all the rest of it, which is great for us, because we will have such a better window into how they're actually doing.

Leah Feiger: Oh, it's amazing.

Sophie Kleeman: Such a better window into how they're actually doing.

Leah Feiger: Also, just because they're so tied up, sourcing inside Anthropic is hard. This is a company that is very much kept to themselves, which is why any kernel of information ... When Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic doomer who bounced out and said, "This really is going to all end the world," and he was on, I don't know, every single talk show or podcast available. One, because of what he was saying, but two, because getting information from inside of Anthropic is difficult. So to your point, a hundred percent. The fact that we're going to have more information there is a game change.

Brian Barrett: The one thing I would add, yes, it's great for us as journalists. We're going to get to see and know so much more information. I'm not as excited about Anthropic now being on this quarterly cycle of needing to demonstrate constant growth and earnings, which is a private company you're shielded from a little bit because the incentives that will make AI profitable are not necessarily the incentives that will make humanity more sustainable, but that's fine.

Sophie Kleeman: Who cares about sustainability? Yep.

Brian Barrett: Who cares? We're all going to be podcasting in caves. Speaking of giant AI companies that are having big moments, good or bad, we've got to talk a little bit about Nvidia. If you're sick of it, totally understand. It's been everywhere, but there are some important updates. Some things have happened just in the last day or two that we should touch on at least quickly. On Tuesday, the company reported its most recent earnings, not surprising that they had another big, big quarter, $115.8 billion in revenue. It's more than six billion ahead of expectations. It was Nvidia's first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned last week after it became public that he had had affairs with a woman suspected of being an asset of Chinese intelligence, and also with at least one of his own direct reports within Nvidia. Over the last few days, we've had a number of Silicon Valley leaders, including, surprise, Elon Musk, campaigning to bring him back. Some have floated the theory that he was set up. Huang himself said in a statement, first statement that he released since this all happened, that he would be honored to return to Nvidia if the board would have him back. Sounds like the board is saying absolutely not. They said that in very clear terms during the earnings call. What do we make of Nvidia in this moment? I should say, too, that we are recording this just after Nvidia's first all hands after Jensen Huang left was led by interim CEO, former CFO, Colette Kress. It's a lot of information. She didn't say much other than, "Hey employees, we're going to give you a lot more money and a lot more stock equity to make you happier so that you don't leave."

Sophie Kleeman: And she kept saying, "We got this," right?

Brian Barrett: She kept saying, “We got this.”

Sophie Kleeman: That was her direct quote, that was her top line, "We're going to be fine. We got this. Do not worry."

Leah Feiger: But so many people just don't think that. I can't stop thinking about what Zoë told us last week, Brian, and the week before. She's been saying this for a while now, just about how Jensen was in such a particular place compared to all of his co-CEOs around Silicon Valley and that he was just not insulated. He was not insulated within his company. He's not the Mark Zuckerberg model at Meta where that guy's not going anywhere. There is just no world where he's getting stripped from his title or responsibilities, which then makes this entire Bring Back Jensen campaign all the more interesting to me, to see Elon Musk and all of these variety of CEOs, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, all of these different people who not even are just kind of quietly commenting on the sidelines, but signing literal petitions saying this. There's an interesting look, at least for me, of the accountability of it all, of is this possible? I guess this is possible. This shouldn't be possible.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm fascinated by this. And Brian, I would love to know what you think is going on here because I sort of though the sharks would be circling in a way, or I thought that they would not want to touch this with a 10-foot pole kind of thing. I mean, I understand that Jensen is just such a sort of crucial part of this ecosystem and Nvidia is such a crucial part of this ecosystem. They've sort of engineered it that way, but I'm curious what you think, what's the vibe? Why are they all coming out so strongly?

Brian Barrett: Oh, because I think that they all see a little bit of themselves in him.

Leah Feiger: He's one of their own.

Brian Barrett: A raconteur, a bad boy about town. And when you are a unique special genius, you should be able to get away with doing whatever else. We talked about this before, it's the idea of separating the art from the artist, but applied to real allegedly scummy behavior, like having sex with a direct report and lying to your board of directors about it. I don't think Jensen's coming back. I'm prepared to be wrong because this industry has done dumber things on shorter timelines, but I do think the board has been so resolute in it. I think Nvidia's going to be fine. This is not a popular take, I think. I think they're going to be fine in the long term. They've got such lock in. They've got customers that don't have anywhere else to turn, and it will be a long time before they do. They may not be as essential a pillar to the US economy and the industry in the long run. Maybe they don't grow quite as fast, but I think that's probably healthy overall. I think a smaller Nvidia with more competition is probably ... I mean, it makes less systemic risk for everybody else. So I think we're going to be OK.

Leah Feiger: One more piece of news before we go to break. President Donald Trump is in Asia this week. He stopped in the Philippines. He's heading to China. He's expected to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday. Right before the trip, the administration said it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China's ability to access advanced AI chips through the use of data centers outside of China's borders. The rule aims to close what a lot of folks in Washington thought was a loophole, basically, which is that Chinese firms are banned from buying the most advanced AI chips made by companies like Nvidia, but they have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers. And this issue became the entire issue this past week because of Nvidia, because Alice Huang was an executive at one of these companies, Megaspeed. WIRED senior correspondent Hugo Lowell has been reporting on what the administration's response has been throughout all of this. And it's been really interesting, honestly, which is for as much as Trump and co are like, "We have to be ahead of China. This is the whole thing. We can't slow down. We can't have guardrails. We have to beat China." There's also been this undercurrent of figuring out how you cooperate, how you're still making money without stifling innovation. This has played out into disputes within Trump's own cabinet. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent versus Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. I have loved the drama of it all.

Sophie Kleeman: The girls are fighting.

Leah Feiger: The girls are fighting. But frankly, for as much as Bessent spent the last week throwing Lutnick entirely under the rug, it kind of turns out, and Hugo found, that Trump has been really playing that middle and siding with Lutnick in a lot of this. So this new rule is going to be really interesting. I'm very curious about it getting enforced. I'm curious about how it's going to also be talked about and communicated this week on the ground actually in China. Hugo's newsletter that published Wednesday night gets into this, and basically what officials have told him quietly is that there probably isn't going to be a lot of movement on AI as Trump arrives, really because of the Nvidia scandal, because there has been so much consternation of quote, unquote Chinese spies everywhere. And this conversation is a little bit at a standstill. So new rule, conversations happening, maybe no results. I don't know. Is that politics as usual? Perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I have a couple questions. One, this is a dumb one, I'm sorry, but we just heard Donald Trump saying, when asked about outages, that if you're big, then people will go for you, even though that has nothing to do with what's going on. So my question, Leah, the eternal question with Donald Trump, how much do we think he actually knows or cares about any of this versus whoever was in the room with him last has told him a thing that sounds good?

Leah Feiger: Oh, I think that's a huge part of it. Ultimately, and I should have this tattooed on my forehead, which is that similar rules to these already existed. They existed in the Biden era. Trump rolled them back in 2025. Again, unclear how much of that context is memorable to the administration or to Trump himself. Fist on table, be competitive. Whether that means we're selling chips or not selling chips, they're not very complicated thoughts. I'm sorry to say. I don't know how else to put it other than I'm not sure that the minutia is that interesting to him. And frankly, the minutia is barely interesting to the rest of us.

Sophie Kleeman: It's deeply unsexy. It's deeply unsexy.

Leah Feiger: It's like every time that we're writing an article on this, and I'm sure that you struggle with this as well, Sophie, I'm like, "And here's our context paragraph where I spell out exactly what Megaspeed meant for chips."

Sophie Kleeman: It reads like a white paper. Yeah.

Leah Feiger: It's horrible. Whereas it's much easier to say, "No, we must be competitive with China. Also, we have to work with China." OK, what does that mean when you're spelling it out?

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, my question too, not to put on my conspiracy theory hat again, but I think-

Brian Barrett: Dit it.

Leah Feiger: This is when we unveil you as our ... This is why you're here.

Sophie Kleeman: Resident conspiracy theorist. I mean, so the reporting about this, it was a little bit hedged. It was like they are moving toward closing a loophole.

Leah Feiger: Yeah.

Sophie Kleeman: So my question is, are they just trying to get out ahead of, they were caught with their pants down in some respects with the Nvidia, the Megaspeed, all that stuff. They've responded with restrictions of their own, rare earth exports et al. So there is this line that they have to draw of, yes, we are anti-China. They have to appease the anti-China hawks in the party while also having to work with the richest nation around. And so it's a very tricky balance.

entries.title: The Best Hatch Black Friday Deals (2026)
entries.summary: Grab the Hatch Sleep Clock for $188 (25 percent off) at Hatch or Amazon through November 30.
entries.content:
If you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking into one bedside gadget. And for the first time, it’s going on sale (early) as a Black Friday deal.

From November 19 through November 20, the Sleep Clock is 25 percent off at Hatch and Amazon. Normally $250, it’s down to $188, which is just $18 more than the Hatch Restore 3’s $170 retail price. And unlike its predecessor, the newer Hatch adds passive sleep monitoring, which is pretty compelling for anyone who hates wearing wearables to bed. Or maybe you’re like me and occasionally forget to wear your Oura Ring to bed, in which case, you wouldn’t have to worry because the Hatch is already quietly tracking your sleep in the background.

Hatch Sleep Clock for $188 ($62 Off)

I’ve been testing the Hatch Sleep Clock for over two months, and it’s earned a permanent spot on my nightstand. As someone who already wears a smart ring and smartwatch to bed, I’m not exactly short on sleep-tracking data. But I’ve never owned a sunrise alarm clock, and I instantly became a convert. Unlike my iPhone or Amazon Echo Dot, it doesn’t wake me up by blaring an obnoxious alarm in my pitch-black bedroom. Instead, it gradually illuminates the room within my scheduled wake-up time. You can customize the sunrise's duration and brightness, and pair it with a soundscape of your choosing. It truly makes getting out of bed feel less jarring, especially as the mornings get darker.

Most notably, the Sleep Clock also doubles as a contactless sleep tracker, using a built-in motion sensor to detect your movements and breathing throughout the night. I compared its readings against my Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12, and while sleep duration estimates were generally aligned, the sleep-stage readings were less consistent. The device doesn’t measure physiological metrics like heart rate, and it can’t detect snoring or other audio-based sleep disruptions. I also found that placement significantly matters. My nightstand tends to collect clutter, so I had to rearrange my trinkets to make room for the clock.

Each morning, the Hatch app gives you a breakdown of when you went to bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and how much time you spent in different sleep stages. The color-coded reports are easy to understand without burying me in random metrics. Plus, unlike most sleep trackers, Hatch doesn't require a subscription to access your sleep data. (You will need that Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) if you want to access the full audio library, however.)

Overall, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the best all-in-one bedside device. I wouldn’t recommend replacing your dedicated wearable with it if detailed health tracking is your priority. But if you’ve been wanting a sunrise alarm clock that can also offer a little insight into your sleep, do not sleep on this Black Friday deal.

More Hatch Deals

If you don’t care for sleep tracking, Hatch is also offering discounts on several other products across its lineup.

entries.title: The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants
entries.summary: In Taiwan, some food vendors are distancing themselves from Nvidia’s former CEO. Others stand by him. “It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire,” says one shop owner.
entries.content:
Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”

Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.

“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.

“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”

Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.

In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars.

The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.

But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business.

The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.

Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”

Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”

entries.title: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
entries.summary: The company’s alternate-universe internet serves as a massive sandbox that allows the Chrome team to properly train AI browsing agents—without the risk of them going rogue.
entries.content:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness,” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed, so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see; the exploration space that we have to address is huge, and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgment when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that, in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode-type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step; there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated, we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

Maybe I'm just a hermit (or maybe everything in NYC is too damned expensive), but some of the most fun I've had in recent memory hasn't been going out. It's been in homes, whether it's for family movie night or for catching up with friends over drinks.

Upgrading your home entertainment setup is more than just buying a new TV or projector. Below are some of the best pieces of WIRED-tested gear to upgrade any home entertainment setup, for yourself or for someone who would be over the moon unboxing a new set of speakers.

Looking for more gifting inspiration? Check out our guides to the Best Gifts for Mom, Best Gifts for Friends, Best Techie Gifts, and Best Gifts for Outdoorsy Folks.

For the Home Theater

It's also a looker, with a silver bezel around the screen that gives the illusion of a metal picture frame. It comes in sizes ranging from 55 inches to 83 inches.

A premium home theater projector can make movies look bigger and better than even some of the best TVs. This Leica Cine Play 1 is a perfect example. Colors pop with vivid clarity, and you can project a 65- to 300-inch image—big enough for even the largest of parties.

Bookshelf speakers have a certain je ne sais quoi about them that other speakers can only dream of. The KEF LSX II have that classy bookshelf look with seriously modern smarts inside. entries.title: Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is
entries.summary: The distance and forces shaping the venerable craft’s trajectory are mind-boggling reminders of the vastness of space.
entries.content:
The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.

It’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

How Do We Measure Distance in Space?

In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

But if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit quickly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

But what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo says in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

OK, So What’s a Light-Day?

As Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

What Forces Affect Voyager 1?

Voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.)

For Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally launched to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really big gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

Will Voyager Go On Forever?

Newton’s second law of motion says that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

Let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

Not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

It’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.

entries.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
entries.summary: Investors betting a barnstorming $107 billion will weigh whether the company’s AI safety strategy and growing public anger toward data centers could impact its growth.
entries.content:
After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”

Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.)

Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.)

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

“Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz says. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”

Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the company offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest company in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.

Updated: 11/19/2026 12:13 p.m. EST This story has been updated to include Anthropic's market debut performance.

entries.title: The Best Early Black Friday Deals on Laptops I’ve Tested (2026)
entries.summary: Some of the best deals on my favorite laptops of the year have already dropped in the lead-up to Black Friday.
entries.content:
It's not Black Friday quite yet, but I'm already on the hunt for Black Friday laptop deals, and this week, they're finally getting good. I know some people will want to wait until the weekend of Black Friday to ensure they're getting the best Black Friday deals, but there's no guarantee that the discounts will stick around until then. I'll be carefully following laptop deals through Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, so make sure to come back for more hand-picked deals on some of the best laptops I've tested this year.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals.

The Biggest MacBook Neo Discount Ever

The MacBook Neo was already cheap, so Apple hasn't been eager to give much in the way of price cuts—despite the laptop having been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo's price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That's a great deal, especially if you're looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren't overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.

An Excellent 15-Inch Laptop for $900

These days, you'll be hard-pressed to find a laptop for under $1,000 that doesn't have any major compromises. That's even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It's a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It's not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, no, but then again, it's hundreds of dollars cheaper.

Microsoft Surface Laptop for $900

It might be well over two years old, but I still find myself recommending the Surface Laptop from 2024. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You're limited to only the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it's the best price I've seen on this laptop this year so far. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

There is a newer version, which comes with the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I've found that it's still quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you're OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you're sold on the more premium design of the Surface Laptop, this is the one to get.

HP OmniBook 5 14 for $750

With the MacBook Neo selling for $649, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $750, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn't seems like a great position to be in for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is on sale often, this is $100 cheaper than I've seen it over the past few weeks.

The HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it's not on sale right now). It's only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.
